lines.text: In 1932, an army major took two machine guns into Australia's wheat fields to fight a bird.
You see, twenty thousand emus were eating the farmers' wheat.
The defence minister said they'd make good target practice.
They even brought a newsreel cameraman.
So Major Meredith rolls in with two soldiers and ten thousand bullets.
On day one, farmers herd the flock toward the guns, and it just splits up.
Two days later, a thousand emus walk straight toward the guns.
He waits until they're close.
Then the gun jams.
So he bolts a gun onto a truck and chases them.
But the truck can't keep up, and the ride is too bumpy to aim.
After six days and twenty-five hundred bullets, the army pulls out.
Back home, people are laughing, and the papers call it the Emu War.
In Parliament, one member mockingly asks if the soldiers will get medals.
So how do you lose a war to a bird?
You see, a machine gun is built for an army standing in a line.
Emus don't do lines.
They split into tiny groups, and every group has one tall bird on lookout.
It's like bowling, if the pins could run.
Round two burns almost ten thousand bullets, and the emus keep eating.
Today, the emu is on Australia's coat of arms.
Undefeated.
